THE SHORT PROPOSAL

A freshness promise
for your mealtime.

Could a promise about usable life before purchase help customers confidently buy for the time they intend to cook?

The customer question

For a planned meal, could a clear promise about usable product life help a customer decide what to buy and when to receive it? The prototype explores that question through cooking-time selection and batch eligibility. Whether the signed-in Licious app already supports this experience remains unverified.

The experience

Let a customer optionally choose when they will cook. Show products and delivery slots that can meet that time using approved batch, storage and quality rules. Reserve an eligible batch and revalidate before accepting the selection.

What the prototype proves

  • A cooking time changes which batch and delivery slot can be promised.
  • The earliest eligible batch is selected, preserving later-dated inventory.
  • A quality hold can invalidate an earlier quote.
  • Reservations, retries and expiry are handled within the demo’s scope.

Hosted: a browser reference model. Downloadable source: Java 21 API, tests and the same UI. All products, prices, dates, buffers and inventory are invented. No revenue effect, production scale or Licious integration has been established.

The business test

Measure delivered-order conversion and repeat purchasing alongside contribution, inventory write-offs, picking constraints and guarantee costs. Treat all benefits as hypotheses until a controlled pilot demonstrates them.

The gate before a pilot

Confirm that this is an unmet customer need, check current app capabilities, and verify that reliable batch data can support the promise. Stop if existing capabilities or unfavorable economics rule it out.

The request

I would value feedback from a product or engineering owner on whether this is a useful problem to investigate. I remain interested in contributing to Licious as a Java Backend Engineer.
